The post OpenAI spent $1.2 million finding nearly 1,000 Linux security flaws. Sam Altman says this is just the beginning. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI spent approximately $1.2 million in API costs to generate working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities. At The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, CEO Sam Altman pointed to those results as an example of what developers could accomplish by spending substantially more on compute to solve difficult engineering problems.

“Apply that to optimizing your code, apply that to solving other hard problems. All that’s coming,” Altman says, appearing alongside OpenAI President Greg Brockman.

The Linux research is part of OpenAI’s broader investment in compute-intensive AI, which includes custom chips, infrastructure, and an agent platform that Altman wants developers to use. He believes the biggest constraint on what these systems can accomplish will be the compute available to run them.

Hunting kernel bugs at scale

In a November 4 technical report titled “A thousand fewer paths to root,” OpenAI says its automated pipeline reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, then generated working exploits for more than half of them.

The agents searched for vulnerabilities, but also, reproduced bugs, tested whether they could be exploited, and wrote patches. Human security researchers reviewed the findings before sending them to Linux kernel maintainers, though OpenAI’s reported numbers do not mean all 948 vulnerabilities have been independently verified or fixed.

The company says the roughly $1.2 million in API spending represents an upper bound because the team had not optimized its harness for cost efficiency.

The results demonstrate how much engineering work agents can perform when given substantial inference budgets. OpenAI is also developing long-running agents that can consume thousands of dollars in compute per day.

OpenAI wants to own the AI stack

“I think we are set up to be like vertically integrated, to deliver the best thing across all the ways people need to use it, and we’re thrilled for people to build very successful businesses on top of us,” Altman says.

OpenAI has spent months investing across custom silicon, computing infrastructure, frontier models, and an agent platform designed to serve consumers and enterprises. The company has also moved further down the stack with its own silicon.

“We are the only company that has the entire intelligence stack.”

Altman made a broader claim about OpenAI’s position in the industry. “We are the only company that has the entire intelligence stack,” he says.

A custom chip for inference

OpenAI’s custom Jalapeño inference chip is already in development, with early reported benchmarks showing gains in throughput per watt and token latency. At DealBook, Altman made an even bigger claim about its potential.

“We have our own chip coming, which is I think going to be the best inference chip in the industry.”

“We have our own chip coming, which is I think going to be the best inference chip in the industry,” Altman says.

The company also wants to bring more of its software offerings together.

“My focus and our focus on product’s been to have one agentic platform that you’re getting everyone to use,” Altman says.

Altman did not announce changes to OpenAI’s developer APIs or restrictions on third-party applications, and he offered few technical details about how the proposed platform would operate.

Compute is the real limiter

Altman believes AI models will become essential to running businesses, but how much companies can do with them will depend on the compute they can access. Recent coding-agent harness comparisons have shown how much execution costs can vary depending on the software surrounding a model.

“I think that the biggest limiter really just will be compute.”

“I think that the economy again is going to be massively accelerated through this technology,” he says. “I think that the biggest limiter really just will be compute.”

item.title: AI needs fresh data. Vector indexing is getting in the way
item.dc:creator: Meredith Shubel
item.description:
It’s not a revelation to say AI workflows are changing enterprise infrastructure. What gets less attention, though, is how they’re

The post AI needs fresh data. Vector indexing is getting in the way appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
It’s not a revelation to say AI workflows are changing enterprise infrastructure. What gets less attention, though, is how they’re also shifting the fundamentals of data processing and search.

The complication lies in the data. As organizations build generative AI (GenAI) applications, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, and AI agents, they’re generating an unwieldy number of vectors from growing volumes of unstructured data. And with all that vectorized data comes a challenge: how to quickly find the right information to power AI applications and workflows. 

“After all, a model can only reason over the context you can find and feed it.”

Whether it’s a RAG system answering a question or an AI agent taking action, enterprise AI applications succeed on retrieval. After all, a model can only reason over the context you can find and feed it. If those systems rely on wrong or outdated information, even the best model can’t fix the underlying context problem. 

But finding the right context inside petabytes of enterprise data is a difficult search problem — one keyword search alone is no match. 

Search has moved beyond keywords

In recent years, search has come a long way from basic keyword-based matching. For one, user behavior has spearheaded a push from simple keyword entries to natural language queries. Agent workloads, meanwhile, which query 10 to 100 times more than humans, bring a new dimension to search — and traditional databases are not prepared to keep up.

While full-text search uses analyzers and relevance tuning to find exact words and phrases that match the index, semantic search goes beyond keywords to focus on meaning and intent, letting users search with everyday language or synonyms instead of exact index terms. Vector search, meanwhile, enables similarity search, using vector embeddings (i.e., numerical representations of data) stored in vector fields to find items that are semantically similar rather than exact matches. 

Hybrid search joins keyword and vector search, letting users combine exact keyword matches with meaning-based searches in a single result set. 

In the new phase of AI adoption, where applications increasingly rely on swathes of unstructured data to retrieve context, traditional keyword search is no longer enough to surface the right information on its own. As a result, organizations are increasingly turning to high-performance vector databases, semantic search, and hybrid search to support new AI workloads. 

Therein lies the next challenge: indexing all those vectors so they can be searched.

Why indexing is the new bottleneck

As organizations move from gigabyte-scale search to petabyte-scale AI workloads, the ability to quickly index vectors has become a major factor in determining whether AI applications have current information to work with. 

The problem is, indexing is often a slow, compute-intensive process, which means it can take days or even weeks for incoming vectors to become searchable. 

“For customers who want to search across petabytes of data, they may notice that it takes days to weeks to index.”

As Rachael Wade, global tech alliances manager at Elastic, tells The New Stack, “For customers who want to search across petabytes of data, they may notice that it takes days to weeks to index.” While a longer indexing timetable may work fine for smaller AI pilots, once it’s time to move those projects into production, indexing delays can significantly stall deployment timelines. 

A big part of the challenge lies in building the vector index, or HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) graph, a layered data structure that connects similar vectors to enable efficient search. During construction, vectors must be compared to determine how they should connect in the graph. Because this process can involve millions or even billions of vectors, building a vector index at enterprise scale is compute-intensive and requires a dizzying number of mathematical operations. 

What happens when enterprises don’t have the compute to keep up? Indexing is slow, so new information takes longer to become searchable, leaving RAG systems, queries, and agents potentially working on stale data. 

“…the new constraint is getting vectors indexed fast enough to keep that search current.”

One example Wade points out to The New Stack is a product catalog, where e-commerce companies rely on fresh data to keep production information up to date and searchable. Manas Singh, technical product manager for accelerated ML and vector search at Nvidia, agrees, adding that, for many companies, “the new constraint is getting vectors indexed fast enough to keep that search current.”

It’s time for GPU-accelerated indexing

While CPUs have been the default for building vector indexes, IT leaders are starting to realize that CPU-based indexing can struggle to meet the scale and data-freshness requirements of modern AI workloads. 

For one, indexing vectorized data at petabyte scale can be painstakingly slow, taking days or even weeks. It’s also costly; when you need to index hundreds of millions or billions of vectors, CPU hardware expenses can add up fast. 

But where CPU-based indexing can be slow and expensive at scale, GPUs are designed for this very kind of large-scale, high-intensity work. For AI workloads with large data volumes and high ingest rates, that makes accelerated computing GPUs built for massive parallelism and high-throughput math ideally positioned for the job. 

At least that’s the idea behind Elastic and Nvidia’s collaboration on GPU-accelerated vector indexing for Elasticsearch. 

The integration is powered by Nvidia cuVS, an open-source NVIDIA CUDA-XTM library for GPU-accelerated vector search and data clustering that enables faster index building and embedding retrieval for AI and recommendation workloads. Elasticsearch accesses cuVS through cuvs-java, another open-source library maintained by Nvidia.

Elastic, for its part, brings semantic and hybrid search to the table via its enterprise-focused vector database — one of the most widely used in the world that powers semantic search, AI assistants, and recommendations for both startups and enterprises. Developers can trial Elasticsearch for free.

By accelerating vector indexing, the Elastic and Nvidia collaboration aims to help enterprises index massive volumes of vectorized data faster so it becomes available sooner for semantic search and AI workloads, including GenAI and AI agents, at speed and scale. 

The payoff of faster indexing can be substantial. Per Elastic, moving indexing construction to GPU with Nvidia cuVS delivers nearly a 12x boost in indexing throughput and a 7x reduction in force-merge latency, i.e., the time it takes to consolidate small index segments.

To put the cost difference in perspective, Wade points to a cost-model example comparing a GPU-based setup with CPU infrastructure. As she tells The New Stack, one GPU, depending on the model, can index hundreds of millions of vectors within a roughly 10-minute SLA. Doing the same work with CPUs, she says, would take about 10 CPUs and require roughly two hours — amounting to what she says is a baseline total cost of ownership savings of 78%. 

The benefits of GPU acceleration become even more pronounced as vector dimensions increase. Because CPUs take significantly longer to process vectors at higher dimensions, GPU acceleration — whether that’s 5x, 6x, 7x, or even 12x — becomes more valuable at larger scales. 

Why faster indexing matters now

For on-premises deployments, Singh also highlights the indirect benefit of lower search latency. 

By shifting indexing work from CPUs to faster, more efficient GPUs, enterprises can free up CPUs for other work, thereby allowing the same on-premises hardware to dedicate more resources to search operations. As Singh puts it: “You free up the CPU resources for other things,” which he says can ultimately lead to lower search latency. 

Meanwhile, because GPU-accelerated vector indexing is available in self-managed Elasticsearch environments, including on-premises, developers can take advantage of faster indexing without having to move workloads off infrastructure they control. 

Altogether, for IT leaders evaluating hardware with an eye on maximizing ROI and maintaining data sovereignty, that means moving indexing from CPUs to GPUs is a triple win: It can complete more indexing work in less time with less infrastructure, while also meeting self-managed, on-premises deployment requirements and freeing up CPU capacity for search. 

In the bigger picture, the move toward GPU-accelerated indexing reflects how AI is changing data processing and search. For RAG systems, AI agents, and other retrieval-dependent applications, getting new data searchable quickly is critical to making those systems truly useful. And that starts with faster indexing.

As vector workloads grow, Elastic and Nvidia are shifting index construction to accelerate AI, boost throughput, improve cost efficiency, and keep data fresh.

item.title: How Orkes ParticleDB turns an impressive demo into a remarkable application
item.dc:creator: Chris J. Preimesberger
item.description:
Building an AI agent that performs an impressive demonstration is one thing. Building one that can reliably process financial transactions,

The post How Orkes ParticleDB turns an impressive demo into a remarkable application appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Building an AI agent that performs an impressive demonstration is one thing. Building one that can reliably process financial transactions, handle customer refunds, or make business decisions without compromising sensitive data is quite another.

That distinction is becoming increasingly important as enterprises move from experimenting with generative AI to deploying agentic applications in production. Developers need more than powerful language models. They need dependable access to enterprise data, orchestration, security, fault tolerance, and a way to explain what an AI agent actually did. Orkes believes its newly previewed ParticleDB can help solve a significant part of that problem.

In an interview last month with The New Stack Editor-in-Chief Nick Lucchesi at AgentCon and MCPCon 2026 in San Jose, California, Orkes co-founder and CEO Jeu George discussed how the company’s emerging database technology and established Conductor orchestration platform are designed to make enterprise AI development simpler and more dependable.

Why ParticleDB matters to developers

At its recent Orkes Shift developer conference in San Francisco, the company previewed ParticleDB, an agentic database designed to bring together data capabilities that conventionally require multiple systems. Enterprise developers frequently work with relational databases, key-value stores, vector databases, and analytical systems. Connecting these technologies often means building complex extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipelines, managing data movement, and maintaining infrastructure that becomes increasingly difficult to operate.

ParticleDB’s premise is that these capabilities should work together within a common engine, reducing the integration burden on development teams. George contends that the need becomes especially pressing when AI agents enter the picture.

“When do AI agents and LLM models become useful? When they have data.”
—Orkes CEO Jeu George

“When do AI agents and LLM models become useful? When they have data,” George told The New Stack. That data, however, often resides within tightly controlled enterprise environments. Companies cannot simply expose sensitive customer information, financial records, or proprietary business processes to autonomous agents.

George envisions a different approach: Rather than allowing agents to roam freely through enterprise systems, a trusted platform supplies the specific information and context they need. Combined with Orkes Conductor, ParticleDB is intended to keep applications, agents and their underlying data closely integrated within customers’ cloud boundaries.

Reliability is still the hardest problem

Beyond data integration, George emphasized a familiar challenge for distributed-systems developers: Things inevitably break. Network outages, software bugs, infrastructure failures, and security incidents are unavoidable. With AI agents potentially executing workflows for hours or even days, recovering from failure without duplicating transactions becomes essential.

“If you design systems from the ground up that things are always going to fail, you simulate failures all the time, and that’s how you get to a robust application.”

“If you design systems from the ground up that things are always going to fail, you simulate failures all the time, and that’s how you get to a robust application,” George said. Orkes Conductor addresses that problem through workflow orchestration, recovery mechanisms, security controls, and audit trails. Developers can combine deterministic business processes with AI-driven decisions while retaining visibility into individual actions.

For regulated industries such as banking and insurance, that visibility is particularly valuable. Organizations need to reconstruct an agent’s decisions, identify which models and systems were involved, and explain outcomes to customers or regulators.

Knowing when to use an agent

One particularly useful part of the conversation examines a straightforward e-commerce refund. George explains why AI agents should handle ambiguous tasks, such as interpreting customer complaints, while predictable operations – issuing refunds, updating financial records and generating receipts – remain conventional workflows. Unusual or high-risk cases can be escalated to humans.

“…successful agentic applications aren’t necessarily the most autonomous. They’re the ones that combine intelligence with dependable execution.”

The broader message for developers is that successful agentic applications aren’t necessarily the most autonomous. They’re the ones that combine intelligence with dependable execution.

Watch our full interview with Jeu George to learn how Orkes is approaching enterprise data integration, agent orchestration, security, and explainability – and why George believes the next generation of AI applications will require a fundamentally different production infrastructure.

item.title: 200 OK is dead as an AI agent health signal. Here’s what comes next.
item.dc:creator: Boris Chabeda
item.description:
A customer asks whether they can swap unworn boots for a size 10. The agent replies, in under a second,

The post 200 OK is dead as an AI agent health signal. Here’s what comes next. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
A customer asks whether they can swap unworn boots for a size 10. The agent replies, in under a second, that it cannot help with that topic. The web service returns 200 OK. Latency is nominal, error counters are flat, and the Datadog dashboard stays solid green. A customer has just left, and nothing in the APM stack knows.

That is the failure this article is about: the kind that looks like success.

In lean manufacturing, this exact category of silent defect is solved using two twin principles: Poka-Yoke (mistake-proofing stations so bad parts cannot pass) and Jidoka (autonomation—building machines that detect anomalies themselves and automatically halt the line via an Andon emergency cord rather than waiting for downstream customer complaints).

“A customer has just left, and nothing in the APM stack knows. That is the failure this article is about: the kind that looks like success.”

Modern AI agent engineering needs to adopt this exact control-loop architecture, replacing passive health checks with active station barriers.

1. Error analysis: Finding what to watch

When we retrospectively ran an offline evaluation benchmark script against three weeks of archived Datadog logs, we found our primary intent classifier had silently dropped 4.2% in schema-valid classification accuracy—masked entirely by default fallback handlers returning 200 OK.

We started by conducting a manual, single-day audit of 100 randomly sampled 200 OK production traces pulled directly from our archived Datadog logs. Two engineers read the raw customer text and manually categorized every routing decision against a ground-truth spreadsheet rubric.

When we bucketed those 100 manual traces, the breakdown was stark:

  • 62% Explicit schema violations / API timeouts: Caught by standard error boundaries or handled by fallback defaults.
  • 11% False negatives: Let spam or out-of-scope queries pass downstream (wasting LLM tokens).
  • 27% False-positive blocks: Valid customer inquiries incorrectly classified as OUT_OF_SCOPE.

This manual audit revealed our critical blind spot. A false negative wastes a few cents in tokens; a schema crash raises a 500 error and pages on-call; but a false-positive block turns away a customer while returning a clean 200 OK. That audit gave us both our core metric to guard—the False Positive Block Rate (FPBR)—and the foundational insight needed to design our observability layer.

2. Why the intent classifier is the blast-radius bottleneck

In our production customer support agent architecture, requests are rarely handled by a monolithic, generalist LLM. Instead, our deployments rely on a multi-agent orchestration pattern (router-specialist topology). An inbound user prompt first hits a triage router agent, which parses the query and dispatches it to downstream domain specialists (Billing, Account Access, Returns), or short-circuits it if it falls outside support bounds (OUT_OF_SCOPE).

Of all the components in this multi-agent stack, we evaluate the Intent Classification Agent first because it sits at the front door.

“An intent classifier false positive has the highest cascading blast radius in the multi-agent topology because it causes a silent, permanent customer drop-off that bypasses all downstream observability.”

If the intent classifier makes a false-positive error—misinterpreting a legitimate exchange or warranty claim as OUT_OF_SCOPE—it triggers an immediate short-circuit. Downstream specialists are never invoked, tokens are saved, and the system cheerfully returns a 200 OK refusal. An intent classifier false positive has the highest cascading blast radius in the multi-agent topology because it causes a silent, permanent customer drop-off that bypasses all downstream observability.

3. Jidoka: Measuring the judge (RoBERTa vs. LLM-as-a-judge)

While the industry frequently defaults to “LLM-as-a-judge” frameworks (using models like GPT-4o or Llama 3) for agent monitoring, we deliberately deployed a fine-tuned encoder model (RoBERTa-base NLI cross-encoder).

To judge an intent classification output, you aren’t asking a model to generate free-form text; you are asking it to evaluate context, verify constraints, and output a strict classification label. Encoders are native classification architectures that look at the entire prompt context multidirectionally rather than predicting the next token autoregressively. This makes them faster, entirely deterministic, free of token-generation overhead, and natively suited for semantic entailment tasks.

Why RoBERTa-base (and when to use DeBERTa instead)

We chose RoBERTa-base specifically for its infrastructure footprint: at ~1.5 GB RAM, it dropped onto our existing c7i.xlarge nodes with zero new cloud cost overhead.

If your customer queries frequently exceed 256 tokens or you are hunting for marginal accuracy gains across enterprise-wide clusters, DeBERTa-v3-base is a better option. DeBERTa’s disentangled attention mechanism yields a 1–2% bump in semantic entailment accuracy. However, that comes at the cost of a heavier CPU compute profile requiring careful thread pinning if co-hosted on legacy nodes alongside core routing services.

Before loading our evaluator in production, we lock PyTorch execution to a single dedicated core and run a container warmup pass to eliminate cold-start latency penalties:

Python
import os
from typing import Any, Dict
from enum import Enum
import torch
from transformers import pipeline

# Lock PyTorch math engine to 1 CPU core before model initialization
torch.set_num_threads(1)
torch.set_num_interop_threads(1)
os.environ["OMP_NUM_THREADS"] = "1"
os.environ["MKL_NUM_THREADS"] = "1"

class AllowedIntent(str, Enum):
    RETURN_POLICY = 'RETURN_POLICY'  # Exchanges classified here
    ORDER_STATUS = 'ORDER_STATUS'
    ACCOUNT_ACCESS = 'ACCOUNT_ACCESS'
    OUT_OF_SCOPE = 'OUT_OF_SCOPE'

class RoBERTaEvaluator:
    """Local, thread-bounded NLI Cross-Encoder Evaluator."""
    def __init__(self, model_path: str):
        self.pipe = pipeline("text-classification", model=model_path, device="cpu")
        self.id2label = self.pipe.model.config.id2label
        
        # Engineering scar: Run dummy inference to force graph compilation during container startup
        self.pipe("warmup prompt")

    def check(self, query: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        res = self.pipe(query[:2000])[0]
        raw_label = res["label"]
        
        if raw_label.startswith("LABEL_"):
            idx = int(raw_label.replace("LABEL_", ""))
            label_name = self.id2label.get(idx, raw_label)
        else:
            label_name = raw_label

        try:
            matched_intent = AllowedIntent(label_name)
        except ValueError:
            matched_intent = AllowedIntent.OUT_OF_SCOPE

        return {"top_intent": matched_intent, "score": float(res["score"])}

To construct our training and validation datasets, we combined our 100 manually audited production traces with 20 synthetic edge cases, yielding a 120-query evaluation dataset partitioned into train, dev, and held-out test splits.

An evaluator is a second opinion, not ground truth. To validate our RoBERTa judge, we evaluated it against our held-out test split of 40 hand-labeled queries (20 positive, 20 negative):

  • True Positive Rate (TPR): 91.5% (sensitivity in catching actual false-positive blocks).
  • True Negative Rate (TNR): 94.0% (specificity in passing valid agent choices).
  • False Alarm Rate (1 – TNR): 6.0% (the baseline overhead sent to the operator queue).

4. The latency budget

Adding inline evaluation on the hot path introduces an immediate engineering anxiety: compute cost and latency.

We ran our classifier on a co-hosted c7i.xlarge instance (4 vCPUs, 8 GB RAM) capable of handling an average baseline of 100 requests per minute (~1.6 req/sec). To ensure our quality gate did not degrade our p95 SLA or starve adjacent services, we constrained the engine using PyTorch CPU optimization guardrails:

  • Model footprint: Fine-tuned RoBERTa-base cross-encoder (~1.5 GB RAM footprint).
  • Thread capping: Bounded to exactly 1 CPU core via torch.set_num_threads(1).
  • Maximum peak load: 480 inference calls per minute (~8 classifications per second). This represents the maximum velocity a single modern Intel thread on the c7i instance can achieve for matrix multiplication on standard-length text prompts (~256 tokens).
  • Latency profile: Evaluator execution takes p50 = 42ms and p95 = 88ms (measured via PyTorch benchmark scripts running synthetic 256-token runs on our co-hosted instance).
  • Financial cost: $0.00 in added cloud infrastructure by reclaiming idle CPU headroom on existing nodes.

5. Control Poka-Yoke: The software limit switch at the station boundary

To fulfill our first Lean requirement, we implement a Control Poka-Yoke as the software equivalent of a manufacturing limit switch that intercepts malformed outputs before downstream tokens are wasted.

Before invoking any classifier, we establish our schema contract:

Python
from typing import Any, Optional, Tuple
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError

class IntentResult(BaseModel):
    selected_intent: AllowedIntent
    confidence: float = Field(ge=0.0, le=1.0)

def validate_schema(raw: Any) -> Tuple[Optional[IntentResult], Optional[Exception]]:
    if not isinstance(raw, dict):
        return None, TypeError('Raw output is not a dictionary')
    try:
        return IntentResult(
            selected_intent=raw.get('intent'),
            confidence=raw.get('confidence', 0.0)
        ), None
    except ValidationError as exc:
        return None, exc

validate_schema() acts as the station sensor: nothing crosses this line unvalidated. If an agent emits a malformed structure, execution immediately branches to an operator handoff without executing downstream steps.

6. Instrumenting the turn: Telemetry, traces, and what an alert looks like

Knowing our judge’s error profile allows us to mathematically derive our trip conditions. Below a 0.9 confidence score, the evaluator’s false-alarm rate spikes above 18%, causing operator fatigue. Therefore, we set our Andon page floor at 0.9.

A single agent turn ties together our previously defined schema validator and RoBERTa evaluator inside a nested OpenTelemetry trace tree. The parent span (intent_agent_turn) encompasses the primary interaction (primary_agent_interaction) and its downstream execution child spans (context_retrieval, prompt_render, llm_inference), followed synchronously by the local judge (nli_evaluation). When the judge detects a semantic mismatch, it triggers an andon_pulled event acting as our digital emergency stop cord:

Python
import hashlib
from typing import Any, Dict
from opentelemetry import trace, metrics

tracer = trace.get_tracer('intent_gate', '1.0.0')
meter = metrics.get_meter('intent_gate', '1.0.0')
disagreements_counter = meter.create_counter('intent_gate.disagreements')

def run_turn(conversation_id: str, query: str, prompt_version: str, agent, evaluator: RoBERTaEvaluator) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    turn = {'prompt_version': prompt_version, 'disagreement_type': None}
    
    with tracer.start_as_current_span('intent_agent_turn') as root:
        root.set_attribute('gen_ai.conversation.id', conversation_id)
        root.set_attribute('app.prompt.version', prompt_version)
        root.set_attribute('app.query.sha256', hashlib.sha256(query.encode()).hexdigest()[:16])

        with tracer.start_as_current_span('primary_agent_interaction') as s1:
            with tracer.start_as_current_span('context_retrieval'): pass
            with tracer.start_as_current_span('prompt_render'): pass
            with tracer.start_as_current_span('llm_inference'):
                raw = agent.classify(query=query, prompt_version=prompt_version)

            result, error = validate_schema(raw)
            s1.set_attribute('app.intent.schema_valid', result is not None)
            if result is None:
                s1.set_status(trace.Status(trace.StatusCode.ERROR, 'schema_violation'))
                turn['action'] = 'HANDOFF_SCHEMA_FAILURE'
                return turn

        with tracer.start_as_current_span('nli_evaluation') as s2:
            verdict = evaluator.check(query)
            agent_intent, eval_intent = result.selected_intent, verdict['top_intent']
            
            dtype = None
            if agent_intent != eval_intent:
                if agent_intent == AllowedIntent.OUT_OF_SCOPE:
                    dtype = 'SUSPECTED_FALSE_POSITIVE'
                elif eval_intent == AllowedIntent.OUT_OF_SCOPE:
                    dtype = 'SUSPECTED_FALSE_NEGATIVE'
                else:
                    dtype = 'INTENT_MISMATCH'

            turn.update({
                'agent_intent': agent_intent.value,
                'evaluator_intent': eval_intent.value,
                'evaluator_score': verdict['score'],
                'disagreement_type': dtype
            })
            
            if dtype:
                disagreements_counter.add(1, {'prompt_version': prompt_version, 'type': dtype})
                s2.add_event('andon_pulled', {'type': dtype})
                turn['action'] = 'HANDOFF_EVALUATOR_DISAGREEMENT'
                return turn

        turn['action'] = 'PROCEED_TO_GENERATION'
        return turn

What the telemetry stack monitors

To maintain complete visibility across the agent’s lifecycle, our telemetry watches four distinct layers across the trace hierarchy:

The first incident: What caught the regression

The first time this observability gate ran in production was during the deployment of prompt version v1.2.0, shipped to tighten return abuse policies. The failure stemmed from a single un-audited prompt modifier that interpreted sizing exchanges as abuse vectors:

Diff
[System Prompt Diff: v1.1.0 -> v1.2.0]

- Handle customer return requests in accordance with standard 30-day policy windows.
+ Zero tolerance for policy circumvention. Intercept all ambiguous customer inquiries 
+ regarding item modification, sizing swaps, or exchanges as potential return abuse vectors.

When a quality regression fires, the alert payload received on the #andon-agent-alerts Slack channel contains the exact trace ID, prompt version tag, candidate classification, and the evaluator’s confidence verdict:

JSON
{
  "event": "QUALITY_REGRESSION_SUSPECTED",
  "trace_id": "37a886864e32af95d4012a30acbda366",
  "prompt_version": "v1.2.0",
  "reason": "EVALUATOR_DISAGREEMENT",
  "disagreement_type": "SUSPECTED_FALSE_POSITIVE",
  "agent_intent": "OUT_OF_SCOPE",
  "evaluator_intent": "RETURN_POLICY",
  "evaluator_score": 0.9412
}

The incident timeline unfolded in under three minutes:

  • 00:00:00: v1.2.0 deployed globally.
  • 00:12:02 (t = 0): The boots query fails 12 minutes after deployment. Agent returns OUT_OF_SCOPE; evaluator flags RETURN_POLICY (score 0.9412).
  • 00:12:04 (t + 2s): #andon-agent-alerts Slack channel receives trace webhook with debug link.
  • 00:14:38 (t + 156s): Traffic auto-drains and reverts to stable v1.1.0 following operator intervention. Total detection-to-reset time: 2m 36s.

The offline evaluation suite missed this failure because its 250 static test cases contained zero colloquial variants for apparel or shoe sizing swaps.

7. Limitations and release provenance protocol

  1. Correlated failure blindspots: If both the primary LLM agent and the RoBERTa evaluator misinterpret a novel phrase identically, no alert fires.
  2. Cold-start vulnerability: The first 30 requests of a new prompt version are unguarded by monitoring thresholds to prevent small-sample noise trips.
  3. Operator dependency: Pulling an Andon cord when no human operators are on duty creates queue backlogs without resolving customer friction.
  4. Prompt version provenance: To prevent unannounced semantic drift, treat prompt text with the same CI/CD immutability as compiled bytecode. Every prompt revision is hashed into deployment manifests, and release notes explicitly log every semantic instruction modifier.

Summary

  • The problem: Production AI agents fail silently by returning confident, well-formed 200 OK refusals that pass passive APM health checks while turning away legitimate customers.
  • The solution: We applied Lean Poka-Yoke (inline schema validation) and Jidoka (a local, thread-bounded RoBERTa-base cross-encoder judge acting as an automated Andon cord) to evaluate intent classifications synchronously.
  • The economics: By locking the evaluator to 1 CPU core (torch.set_num_threads(1)) on co-hosted c7i.xlarge nodes, we achieved p50 = 42ms / p95 = 88ms latency with $0.00 in added cloud infrastructure cost.
  • The incident: When prompt v1.2.0 accidentally flagged product sizing swaps as out-of-scope, the inline judge caught the regression at t=0, alerted #andon-agent-alerts via Slack webhook at t+2s, and enabled a full rollback to v1.1.0 within 2 minutes and 36 seconds.

The post 200 OK is dead as an AI agent health signal. Here’s what comes next. appeared first on The New Stack.
200 OK hides silent AI agent failures. Catch false-positive customer refusals using Lean Jidoka principles and a local RoBERTa evaluator.

item.title: S3 vs. ScyllaDB for tiny telemetry: What Red Canary learned the hard way
item.dc:creator: Cynthia Dunlop
item.description:
At Red Canary, storing large amounts of small data is a big deal.  Their Linux Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR)

The post S3 vs. ScyllaDB for tiny telemetry: What Red Canary learned the hard way appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
At Red Canary, storing large amounts of small data is a big deal. 

Their Linux Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) sensors run on hundreds of thousands of endpoints (VMs, laptops, EC2 instances, etc.) They continuously generate small payloads with telemetry details (file changes, process launches, and network connections), as well as self-reported health checks. Uploading all these small payloads to S3, which charges per PUT operation, became quite costly at scale.

The logical approach – merging data into larger chunks before uploading them to S3 — did cut costs. However, it also introduced file-size limits, delayed data freshness, and complicated debugging of specific endpoint records. After some experimentation, they cut latency and costs with an unexpected approach: storing large amounts of small data in a write-optimized database, ScyllaDB.

“After some experimentation, they cut latency and costs with an unexpected approach: storing large amounts of small data in a write-optimized database, ScyllaDB.”

Andres Medina, a staff software engineer on the LinuxEDR team, took the Monster Scale Summit stage to share their journey from S3 and Postgres to a Firehose buffer to ScyllaDB – and the lessons learned along the way. You can watch his complete talk or read the highlights below. 

Checking the health check data flow 

Medina’s team decided to start pipeline optimization with the health check data. As a lower-risk part of the pipeline than the actual telemetry data, it seemed like the safest spot for experimentation. 

Problem 1: cost

The cost problem was the most pressing pain that they wanted to address. “S3 charges a flat fee per S3 PUT, which occurs for every payload upload,” Medina explained. “So if we have hundreds of thousands of endpoints, we’re being charged for hundreds of thousands of S3 PUTs.”

They hoped that creating a buffer would provide a short-term fix, at least. Using AWS Firehose and Kinesis, they combined small data streams into larger files and wrote them to S3 once they reached a defined threshold. It did reduce costs – but at the cost of introducing new issues:

  • Firehose and Kinesis impose a strict one-megabyte-per-shard limit, and the larger files just didn’t fit. 
  • Visibility into the health data was delayed. Before, it was passed over to S3 immediately. With the change, they had to wait until the designated threshold was met. 
  • Debugging specific endpoints became difficult. When lots of endpoint IDs are mashed together, it’s much harder to find a particular endpoint in a large customer fleet.

Problem 2: database scalability

Another issue: Postgres was used to store endpoint metadata, and it was just overwhelmed at their scale. “Sometimes a large customer might restart a chunk of their fleet,” Medina shared. “That means that many endpoints will try to check in at very similar times, causing a spike of writes in the database.”  They also had to throttle their incoming database requests, as sudden bursts could take down the database. 

Yes, they could have tweaked and tuned their existing database for yet more short-term solutions. But the team wanted a longer-term fix. 

Looking for a longer-term solution 

The team set the following criteria for a new approach:

  • Ability to sustain their large and growing throughput
  • Improve time-to-visibility in their portal 
  • Minimal admin burden 

They ultimately chose ScyllaDB Cloud, with the Bring Your Own Account (BYOA) deployment option. Medina explained, “We installed it in our own AWS account, in a separate account from our remaining data to reduce any risk there. That way, ScyllaDB can still manage that cluster without having access to our data.”

Their shift to ScyllaDB involved two phases: replacing Postgres, then replacing S3. 

Replacing Postgres

Replacing Postgres was simpler than replacing S3. Each sensor event appends a single row, and the web portal always queries it in a time series manner – asking for a customer’s active endpoints over a given period of time. Still, Postgres and ScyllaDB are very different databases, which pushed the team to learn a few lessons regarding tombstones and uneven data volumes.

When you delete data in ScyllaDB, it isn’t just removed. ScyllaDB leaves a timestamped marker called a tombstone. This prevents data resurrection, which occurs if a node misses a deletion (e.g., due to a network error) and later restores the old data during a cluster repair.

Tombstones were particularly troubling for Red Canary’s ephemeral endpoints, which are online only for a short time. Medina said, “Some clusters might scale up for an hour and then scale back down, which means an endpoint is alive for a very small amount of time. That meant some customers had partitions that were mostly just tombstones. When you query it, ScyllaDB has to iterate through all these tombstones, making our latency worse than it should be.”

The fix here was simple. Since they don’t need to delete any data, they didn’t need tombstones. They cleared them from the read path by setting a short TTL on the table and tuning tombstone garbage collection to evict tombstones faster. The latency improved as a result.

“Some clusters might scale up for an hour and then scale back down. That meant some customers had partitions that were mostly just tombstones. When you query it, ScyllaDB has to iterate through all these tombstones, making our latency worse than it should be.”

The second issue was that their data volume varied wildly across customers. Some customers have a few dozen endpoints, while others have hundreds of thousands. To avoid creating hot partitions in ScyllaDB, Medina and the team developed a bucketing strategy.

They split each customer’s data into smaller numbered “buckets,” which ScyllaDB distributes across shards. When fetching a customer’s data, the system checks how many buckets they have and queries them all at once (in parallel) for faster responses.

The following diagrams compare the short-term solution to the long-term one. In the After diagram, the Postgres endpoint database is gone. Instead, the service forwards sensor health data to ScyllaDB, and the portal queries the service for the metadata needed for recently active endpoints.

Replacing S3 

The next challenge was the unconventional move to replace S3 usage with ScyllaDB. Throughput was higher, and access patterns were less predictable. Medina explained, “It’s not a service trying to query in one way. Instead, it’s developers debugging.” They could predict one thing at least: developers would debug one specific sensor at a time. So, they defined “sensor ID” as the partition for their queries. 

There was an ulterior motive here. Medina shared, “One of our biggest reasons for wanting to do this was to see if ScyllaDB could also be used for our detection data in the future.” Since the health data had similar throughput and was less critical to their operations, it was a safe way to test the waters for a broader shift to ScyllaDB.

The first complicating factor in the S3 replacement was that their events contain very large arrays used to track a given process’s memory consumption at a given endpoint. Some endpoints have thousands of processes running at the same time, which could create rather large rows. The solution was to unnest the array and store it in an auxiliary table, tracking each process’s memory usage separately from the primary table. “We can still put every row in the same partition so that our querying is still easy enough, as long as the partition doesn’t get too big (too many rows),” Medina added.

Next up: batching. They wanted to batch rather than write each health event individually to avoid multiple network round trips to the database. However, batching is more efficient if every statement in a batch belongs to the same partition. Ideally, they split each health payload’s statements by partition when they receive it. The ScyllaDB Rust driver wasn’t designed for this, though.

Wrangling the Rust driver

More specifically, the Rust driver doesn’t expose a prepared statement with values already serialized (a bound statement). To get a partition for a statement with values, you would have to serialize it once to get the corresponding hashed token, then serialize it again to execute the statement. 

If you try to keep these values unserialized together with the statement, it’s difficult to put them into collections in Rust (a Rust collection like a vector or hash map requires everything to be the same type). If different statements have different types, it’s complicated. However, once you serialize them, those values are just a stream of bytes. You can keep all that data in the same collection.

Medina detailed his workaround like this: “To get around this, I forked the Rust driver to add the idea of a bound statement and then a bound batch, which is just a collection of statements. With this now in place, we can ask the bound statement what its token is without having to reserialize it, and then execute it again without reserializing it. A second benefit is that we can separate CPU work from I/O work. In Rust, you mostly use Tokio for I/O operations, and doing CPU work there can block the runtime and reduce efficiency. 

“When we made this change, our average time to process a file dropped from about 150 milliseconds to 50 milliseconds — a drop of about 60%.”

So now we can do all of the CPU work in a CPU-bound worker using Rayon, and then we send it back to Tokio when we’re done. Then in Tokio, you can just do the I/O for the batch execution. When we made this change, our average time to process a file dropped from about 150 milliseconds to 50 milliseconds — a drop of about 60%. Of course, this is for our use case, so your mileage may vary.”

Did it work?

Here’s the final system architecture. 

The LinuxEDR services now own the health data for the LinuxEDR product, and that data no longer goes to the engine. ScyllaDB stores all the check-ins and health metrics. There’s a separate metrics database for now, but that might be replaced soon. The portal can query the services to get the list of active endpoints, and any developer can query ScyllaDB for debugging.

So far, the team has significantly reduced their per-endpoint cost. Batching has boosted their I/O per second, with a ~20X reduction in writes versus rows inserted (~670K rows/second, but only ~36K writes/second due to batching).  And the portal now retrieves endpoints in seconds instead of minutes for its largest customers. “Each query to ScyllaDB is in the double-digit millisecond range,” Medina noted. 

Next steps 

Medina wrapped up with this: 

“Since the transition has gone fairly smoothly, we’re now exploring using it for data that is more critical. One of my team’s main goals is to store our detection data in ScyllaDB to avoid sending data that doesn’t need to go to the engine. Also, we’re looking at ways to use it outside my team to replace some uses of OpenSearch, which has been giving us issues with cost, performance, and sometimes paging…no one likes being paged. Ideally, I would also like to merge the fork at some point so I don’t need to rebase the driver on every new release.”

The post S3 vs. ScyllaDB for tiny telemetry: What Red Canary learned the hard way appeared first on The New Stack.
Red Canary replaced S3 and Postgres with ScyllaDB to handle tiny telemetry payloads at scale, slashing costs and query times.

item.title: Why verification, not generation, is your secret to AI coding ROI
item.dc:creator: Anirban Chatterjee
item.description:
For two years, the question around AI coding was whether agents could write good code. Developers have largely answered it:

The post Why verification, not generation, is your secret to AI coding ROI appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
For two years, the question around AI coding was whether agents could write good code. Developers have largely answered it: AI now generates or significantly assists 65% of the code they commit, according to Sonar’s 2027 State of Code Developer Survey. A year ago that figure was 42%, and this year’s number matches what respondents then expected to see a year later. Clearly, adoption is outrunning expectations.

“Clearly, adoption is outrunning expectations.”

This is because AI tools are getting better at coding, as shown by the increase in effectiveness our survey respondents (1,026 developers and engineering managers) reported alongside their increased adoption. The harder question is whether teams can trust what the agents ship. For most respondents, the report suggests the answer is “not quite yet,” but things are moving in the right direction.

The verification gap

Four numbers describe the problem:

  • 53% spend more time reviewing code than creating it, compared to 18% before adopting AI tools.
  • Despite this, 76% can’t verify code as fast as AI generates it
  • 94% don’t fully trust that AI-generated code is functionally correct.
  • However, only 39% always check AI-generated code before committing it, down from 48% last year. 

As adoption of coding agents continues to increase, this is now happening in systems that matter. Seventy-six percent say their team or company uses AI coding tools for business-critical or mission-critical services, a 31% increase from last year. 

The bottleneck moves downstream.

When code generation becomes abundant, review becomes the constraint. Left alone, it fails in one of two ways: reviews get stuck in a queue that eats the productivity gains, or verification quietly gets skipped. The data shows signs of both.

The side effects show up in the codebase too. Half of respondents say AI has produced unnecessary or duplicative code, and 34% report code that is hard to maintain or refactor. The share who say AI-generated code has made outages more frequent doubled, from 6% to 12%. Interestingly, 36% and 35% respectively say AI reduced outage frequency and reduced outage severity.

“When code generation becomes abundant, review becomes the constraint. Left alone, it fails in one of two ways: reviews get stuck in a queue, or verification quietly gets skipped.”

Security is more mixed. Concerns are shifting from vulnerabilities created in code touched by AI to vulnerabilities discovered in shipped code by bad actors with AI’s help. Respondents more often say AI-generated code reduced vulnerabilities than increased them (28% versus 15%). But 61% are very or extremely concerned that AI-powered attackers will find and exploit vulnerabilities faster and at greater scale.

Software factories raise the stakes

The pressure is about to increase with software factories: an environment where agents work autonomously on tasks. Thirty-four percent expect their teams to build or use agentic software factories within a year, compared with 5% today — that’s roughly a sevenfold jump.

A human reading every diff at the end of the pipeline does not scale to that model. If the volume of change grows by an order of magnitude and the review process stays the same, it’s unclear how confidence in code can realistically be established. For most organizations, this is because they don’t have the right pieces in place: 55% report AI-specific guidelines, policies, or quality gates, but only 23% describe those controls as well-defined and distinct, or automated.

Engineering confidence into the factory

Confidence has to be built into the system from the start; the survey results point to four priorities that organizations should implement to achieve this:

1. Intent: define the outcome before the agent starts. 37% name unclear requirements as a top source of toil, and 26% cite correcting or rewriting AI-generated code. Agents should have explicit business objectives, architecture standards, quality criteria, and security requirements to deliver against. Teams then have a basis for judging the result.

2. Guiderails: guide and govern agents as they work. Teams that give coding agents clear standards and controls are more likely to report 50%+ ROI than teams with few controls (32% versus 19%). In practice, that means supplying context and rules while the code is written, and setting limits on tool access and permissions.

3. Verification: check every change independently. 77% say strong verification tools increase their trust in AI code. Inline checks matter too; teams using automated review as AI code is written more often report positive security impacts than those without it (61% versus 46%). Independent checks and fixes before release are what separate code that is correct from code that merely looks correct.

“Independent checks and fixes before release are what separate code that is correct from code that merely looks correct.”

4. Evidence: make confidence measurable and auditable. If you can’t show what you checked, what you found, and what you fixed, you can’t defend a release decision or prove the investment paid off. But only 36% say their team measures AI’s productivity impact and can see the results. Forty-seven percent expect an ROI of 50% or more, but only 27% report achieving it, and 22% can’t say what return AI coding has delivered. 

Build confidence before scaling autonomy

The teams leading the charge are showing the way to AI-assisted software engineering by implementing code confidence. You can start with the agents already in your workflows: make requirements explicit, enforce boundaries and standards, check changes early and independently, and retain the evidence behind every decision. Engineers remain responsible for setting those standards and exercising the judgment that AI can’t replace.

As agents become more capable, the test of progress should not be how much code they produce or how little human involvement they require. It should be whether teams can deliver useful software faster without compromising security, reliability, or maintainability. Code confidence is what connects greater autonomy to that outcome: a consistent basis for deciding what is ready to ship, even as the tools doing the work change.

The post Why verification, not generation, is your secret to AI coding ROI appeared first on The New Stack.
AI helps write 65% of code, but developer trust lags. Learn how to close the verification gap and build confidence in Sonar's 2027 survey.

item.title: “Collaboration over competition”: Hugging Face hands model inference traffic to OpenRouter
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
Hugging Face and OpenRouter have announced a partnership that promises to make AI model inference faster and more reliable for

The post “Collaboration over competition”: Hugging Face hands model inference traffic to OpenRouter appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Hugging Face and OpenRouter have announced a partnership that promises to make AI model inference faster and more reliable for developers.

The collaboration, announced by the two companies on Monday, will see Hugging Face use OpenRouter’s infrastructure to route language-model requests to third-party providers based on pricing, performance and reliability.

Previously, Hugging Face used its own routing system, introduced as part of its Inference Providers service in January 2025, to connect developers with companies running AI models. The service initially launched with four providers: Fal, Replicate, SambaNova and Together AI. The system would select a provider to handle each request, but if that provider encountered a problem, the request failed.

With OpenRouter now in the mix, the request can automatically be passed to another provider, meaning that developers should encounter fewer failed requests.

Hugging Face co-founder and CEO Clément Delangue sees the partnership as an example of how collaboration between AI companies can make open-weight models more accessible to developers, with each company focusing on its own strengths.

“Too many people treat AI as a zero-sum race. Open-source is winning by doing the opposite: collaboration over competition!”

“Too many people treat AI as a zero-sum race,” Delangue writes on LinkedIn. “Open-source is winning by doing the opposite: collaboration over competition!”

“Hugging Face for storage and collaboration. OpenRouter for inference,” he adds.

Stripe, Nvidia and the bigger picture

The announcement comes less than a week after Stripe completed its acquisition of OpenRouter, a deal first announced in August and reportedly worth more than $7 billion.

Hugging Face, for its part, is also in the process of being acquired by AI chip giant Nvidia for nearly $13 billion. Nvidia, however, is currently grappling with a scandal involving its former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week amid the controversy.

At any rate, the OpenRouter integration is already live, initially covering 160 models from 38 AI labs. For Hugging Face, the arrangement means it can offer developers more dependable access to these models without having to maintain its own routing system.

In real terms, this means that users can continue chatting directly with AI models on Hugging Face’s model pages, while new interface features let them compare providers by price, speed and uptime, and check performance metrics to help them choose a provider.

The integration also works in reverse. OpenRouter users can now send records of their AI model requests to Hugging Face Storage Buckets, where they can examine prompts and responses, build evaluation datasets and prepare models for fine-tuning.

Zooming out, OpenRouter gains a direct route into Hugging Face’s enormous developer community, potentially bringing more inference traffic — and revenue –to its new owner, Stripe.

Looking ahead, Hugging Face says it plans to let developers connect their OpenRouter accounts directly to Hugging Face, while expanding the integration to cover more AI tasks. It hasn’t provided a timeline for either development.

In a blog post announcing the tie-up, OpenRouter’s director of product marketing Sasha Blumenfeld says the partnership builds on the company’s original mission of simplifying access to AI models.

“We built OpenRouter so developers can reach many models and providers through one API, use the best model for each task, and count on it to respond.”

“We built OpenRouter so developers can reach many models and providers through one API, use the best model for each task, and count on it to respond,” Blumenfeld writes. “Starting today, that extends to everyone building on Hugging Face.”

How OpenRouter chooses providers

The integration builds on a recent routing overhaul OpenRouter announced in October, which changed the criteria its infrastructure uses to determine where inference requests are sent.

Rather than relying primarily on advertised prices, the system continuously monitors providers’ actual performance, weighing response times, costs and availability before choosing where to send each request. If a provider becomes overloaded or stops responding, OpenRouter can shift traffic elsewhere and automatically retry failed requests with another provider.

OpenRouter says the changes reduced capacity-related errors by 46%, shortened the wait for the first generated token by 16.9%, and increased token generation speed by 16.3% in one of its tests. There was a cost, however: the average price per request rose by 6%, though these figures relate specifically to OpenRouter’s routing overhaul in October.

Fast-forward to today, and developers using Hugging Face can now choose whether to prioritize lower costs or faster responses, or leave OpenRouter to decide. The interface also shows the companies available to run each model, alongside their respective prices, speeds and recent availability, allowing developers to compare their options before making a request.

Developers can also disable individual providers in their account settings, preventing requests from being sent to those companies. Organizations can apply the same restrictions across all requests billed to them.

There is one notable catch in all of this: developers can no longer use their own third-party provider API keys for language-model requests through Hugging Face. Those requests must now be billed through Hugging Face, although developers can still select particular providers.

Hugging Face says it will continue charging the underlying providers’ prices without adding a markup.

It’s worth noting that the integration currently applies only to language models. Image, video and audio generation continue using Hugging Face’s existing infrastructure.

The rise of open-weights

The backdrop to all this, of course, is the rapid rise of open-weight models as more cost-effective alternatives to those emerging from the trillion-dollar frontier AI labs.

Back in September, The New Stack reported that open-weight models accounted for 60% of OpenRouter’s US token consumption in August, with Chinese-developed models responsible for most of that traffic.

That same month, another milestone emerged: open-weight models had processed a majority of tokens on Vercel’s AI Gateway for the first time, accounting for 56% in August, up from just 7% in December 2025. However, they represented only 14% of estimated spending, while Anthropic alone accounted for 64%.

The trend has very much continued, too. According to OpenRouter’s October analysis, open-weight models accounted for 71.7% of tokens processed by its 50 most-used models at the end of September, up from 26.8% a year earlier. Over that period, weekly token consumption for open-weight models grew more than sixtyfold.

Vercel’s October AI Gateway report painted a similar picture, with open-weight models accounting for 71.5% of tokens in September. Their share of estimated spending also climbed to 23%, although proprietary models continued to account for most of the money flowing through the platform.

“The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.”

In a blog post announcing its partnership with OpenRouter on Monday, Hugging Face argued that developers don’t always need the most capable AI models, particularly when cheaper alternatives can handle their tasks adequately. It noted that open-weight models cost roughly four times less on average than proprietary alternatives.

“The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks,” the company writes. “For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.”

For Hugging Face and OpenRouter, the growing appetite for open-weight models creates an opportunity to capture more of that demand, with developers able to choose between competing providers based on cost and performance.

The post “Collaboration over competition”: Hugging Face hands model inference traffic to OpenRouter appeared first on The New Stack.
Now owned by Stripe, OpenRouter is helping Hugging Face deliver more reliable access to open-weight language models. But custom provider keys are out.

item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell

The same AI model can cost up to five times more to run depending on the coding agent harness it’s

The post Your AI coding agent could cost 5x more depending on the harness, benchmark finds appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
The same AI model can cost up to five times more to run depending on the coding agent harness it’s paired with, according to a new benchmark that tested 22 configurations across five open-weight models.

Runta and Baseten ran those combinations 27,280 times for FrontierHarness Eval v1.1, consuming roughly 83 billion tokens in the process.

Nearly 65% of estimated inference spending went to runs that failed verification or timed out.

The model itself accounted for 92.8% of the cost differences, but the harness still made a considerable difference. One configuration could be the cheapest option for one model and among the most expensive for another, adding another wrinkle for developers looking to cut coding-agent costs by changing harnesses or swapping in a cheaper model. Nearly 65% of estimated inference spending went to runs that failed verification or timed out.

Rankings flip with the model

The benchmark covered 22 coding-agent harness configurations across five models served through Baseten, including GLM-5.3, GLM-5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Muse Spark Open, and Kimi-K3. Each configuration ran 62 terminal-based tasks four times per model, with pass rates, inference costs and execution times recorded for comparison.

Codex CLI ranked first for lowest average cost per task with GLM-5.3 but dropped to 16th out of 22 configurations with Kimi-K3. DeepSeek Harness Creator showed an even larger change, ranking first with Muse before falling to 21st with GLM-5.3 Flash.

Across the five models, harnesses shifted a median of 11 ranking positions when the model changed, while costs varied by as much as fivefold even when the model stayed the same.

Across the five models, harnesses shifted a median of 11 ranking positions when the model changed, while costs varied by as much as fivefold even when the model stayed the same. The biggest difference came with DeepSeek, where Cline CLI cost five times as much as OpenCode v1 but delivered a pass rate only two percentage points higher.

The researchers also shuffled the trials within each model 300 times to see whether random variation could explain the cost differences. The gaps in the actual results were larger than those in the shuffled trials, with a reported p-value of 0.003.

Failed runs eat the budget

Failed runs accounted for 52.7% of estimated inference spending, with timeouts adding another 11.8%. Just 35.5% went toward successful runs. Those costs are based on Baseten’s published rates, but they put a price on a familiar problem with coding agents struggling to complete difficult tasks.

Among the five best-value harnesses, 68% to 82% of unsuccessful runs ended with the agent submitting a final answer that failed verification rather than timing out.

The researchers also found 216 instances of reward hacking in the execution logs, including 163 involving online lookups. All received zero scores.

Steps, not prompts, drive cost

Runta looked at whether prompt size, tool count, cache hit rates, or agent steps had the biggest impact on cost. Step count was the only factor with a statistically significant correlation to cost per successful task, at 0.51.

Mini-SWE-agent showed how multi-step agent execution can drive up token costs, starting with the smallest prompt in the benchmark at 882 tokens but averaging 38 steps per successful task and ranking 17th out of 22 configurations for cost per pass.

The five best-value harnesses relied heavily on shell commands, which made up 61% to 93% of their tool calls, and rarely used subagents, or context summarization. Runta didn’t test those design choices separately, however, so the results don’t establish whether the simpler setups were responsible for the lower costs.

item.title: OpenAI’s own tests show GPT-6.2 Astra is twice as likely to hide coding failures
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
OpenAI’s new GPT-6.2 Astra is nearly twice as likely as its predecessor to leave users unaware of problems that prevented

The post OpenAI’s own tests show GPT-6.2 Astra is twice as likely to hide coding failures appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI’s new GPT-6.2 Astra is nearly twice as likely as its predecessor to leave users unaware of problems that prevented it from finishing a coding task, according to the company’s own safety evaluations. Developers building autonomous agents could encounter the same problem, since OpenAI has added a mitigation to Codex that isn’t automatically applied to direct API requests.

In its GPT-6.2 system card, published Tuesday alongside the release of GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, OpenAI reported that Astra failed to disclose a known obstacle in 22.28% of evaluated coding tasks, compared with 11.09% for GPT-6 Astra.

An agent may write better code without telling the developer when it couldn’t finish the job.

The company says both models perform better on demanding tasks while using fewer output tokens, but those improvements don’t necessarily make them more reliable at reporting failures. An agent may write better code without telling the developer when it couldn’t finish the job.

The New Stack has asked OpenAI whether it plans to extend the Codex mitigation to API developers and how the additional instructions affect the models’ failure-reporting behavior.

Inside the blocker deception test

OpenAI measured the behavior with an internal evaluation called Blocker Deception, which gives models realistic coding assignments before deliberately introducing obstacles that make the requested work impossible to finish as specified.

In some runs, the evaluation removes a source file the agent was supposed to modify. In others, it disables a tool needed to build the project. The evaluation then checks whether the model tells the user what happened or leaves the obstacle out of its final response.

The caveats Astra leaves out

The company acknowledges the regression and says it is still investigating the cause. One possible explanation is that training the models to give shorter answers with fewer caveats may have made them less likely to report problems that prevented them from completing a task. OpenAI cautions that the evaluation was designed to trigger this behavior, so the results don’t necessarily reflect how often Astra misleads users in production.

A separate evaluation, Broken Search Tool, identified a similar problem. The model receives questions requiring information retrieval while the necessary search capability is disabled. GPT-6.2 Astra failed to acknowledge the missing requirement or unavailable tool in 23% of cases, compared with 7.58% for GPT-6 Astra and 1% for GPT-6.1 Terra.

Developers can check the logs, test results, and git diff … but they shouldn’t have to dig through an entire session to find out that something failed.

Developers can check the logs, test results, and git diff to see what an agent actually did, but they shouldn’t have to dig through an entire session to find out that something failed. If an agent says it finished the job without mentioning a missing dependency or a failed build, that work could make it through review without anyone realizing there’s a problem. It’s another example of the code confidence gap that becomes harder to manage as agents take on more work across a repository.

The fix the API misses

OpenAI says it developed a prompt-based intervention that substantially reduced the rate of omitted blockers in evaluations of both Astra and Sol. The company incorporated that intervention into the standard Codex developer prompt at launch, but it does not automatically apply the same instructions to direct API requests.

Codex users get the updated prompt, but developers building their own agents through the API don’t.

Codex users get the updated prompt, but developers building their own agents through the API don’t. OpenAI hasn’t shown whether adding similar instructions to a custom harness would produce the same results.

The harness can’t take the model’s completion summary at face value because it needs to verify the diff, check test results, and confirm the expected artifacts exist before marking a task complete.

These verification loops are especially important for unattended agents, where a failed step can go unnoticed until someone reviews the work.

Performance up, reporting down

The disclosure comes as OpenAI promotes improvements in coding performance and efficiency across both new models.

In its launch announcement, OpenAI said GPT-6.2 Sol came within 0.5 points of Astra on Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 coding benchmark at approximately one-fifth the estimated cost per task, with both models running at maximum effort.

In testing shared with The New Stack by OpenAI, Replit reported that GPT-6.2 Sol passed more tests, used 62% fewer output tokens and ran nearly three times as fast as GPT-6.1 Sol when building software from scratch.

Faster execution and lower inference costs make these models appealing for automated coding, but OpenAI’s safety tests show that better performance doesn’t necessarily mean an agent will tell developers when something goes wrong.

The post OpenAI’s own tests show GPT-6.2 Astra is twice as likely to hide coding failures appeared first on The New Stack.
OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra stays quiet about coding failures more often than the model it replaces, and Codex’s fix skips API developers.

item.title: Microsoft’s new coding model promises near-Opus performance at 5% of the cost
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
At its Ignite conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, Microsoft announced a number of new AI models, including two new

The post Microsoft’s new coding model promises near-Opus performance at 5% of the cost appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
At its Ignite conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, Microsoft announced a number of new AI models, including two new coding models.

Imaginatively named Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, these new models promise to come very close to models like GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 at less than half the cost.

As Microsoft notes, “MAI Code 2 is at the frontier of price-performance” for enterprise coding tasks. “It does all of this while also delivering changes code maintainers would merge, at a fraction of frontier cost.”

MAI Code 2 benchmarks

The promise here is that Code 2 gets to 98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the cost and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost (which also goes to show how expensive Anthropic’s models are to run right now).

The model, Microsoft says, has also been tuned to create “great dashboards and visualizations” and that it “excels at visual coding.”

At least for the OpenAI comparison, it’s worth noting that OpenAI today released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, with improved performance. That softens Microsoft’s claims a bit, but it’s worth noting that OpenAI, too, notes that at least on Agents’ Last Exam, GPT-6.2 Astra is now 5.5 points “ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost” (which also goes to show how expensive Anthropic’s models are right now).

MAI Code 2 Flash benchmarks

As for MAI Code 2 Flash, Microsoft argues that it can match Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna on benchmarks like DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal-Bench 2.1, and SWE Atlas at 20% and 65% of the cost, respectively.

Microsoft’s bet: specialist models vs. generalists

One interesting wrinkle here is that Microsoft specifically tuned these models for the day-to-day coding work of its users. “They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work,” Microsoft writes.

The models Microsoft is comparing these models to are generalists. For a while, OpenAI took a similar approach with its Codex models, but it has abandoned this approach in favor of more general models.

Microsoft, meanwhile, which doesn’t build those kinds of in-house frontier models, seems to be focused on smaller specialized models that it can run more efficiently. And while they won’t match the frontier models across every benchmark, focusing on these specific tasks makes a lot of sense in this context.

Microsoft is taking this even further with models like MAI Work Flash, a model trained to work across Microsoft 365 and Fabric IQ products.

Availability

MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash are now available in GitHub Copilot, while Code 2 Flash is in limited preview on Microsoft Foundry. OpenRouter, Vercel, Hermes, Open Code, and Kilo will soon get support as well.
